anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between the physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns forces inefficient execution paths regardless of optimizer decisions.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Exhaustion of kernel-enforced resources (file handles, shared memory, semaphores, threads, address space, cgroup quotas) restricts the database’s ability to create or use essential operating-system objects.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Saturation or exhaustion of network paths, sockets, listener backlogs, or authentication/connection slots prevents timely establishment and servicing of client connections.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from sub-optimal physical schema/index design, hard OS-level resource ceilings, and constrained network/connection capacity. Inefficient queries generated by the poor schema design intensify demand on back-end processes, file descriptors, shared memory, and socket endpoints, while limited kernel quotas and network bottlenecks block the system from scaling or recovering, leading to cascading service degradation.

Combined phenomena:  • Queries run slowly due to full scans and excess row fetches, keeping server processes busy longer and accumulating large result sets.  • Backend processes and parallel workers linger in client read/write waits because network throughput is insufficient; socket queues fill, and TCP retransmits rise.  • Connection attempts start timing out or returning "too many connections" or "cannot allocate file descriptor/shared memory" errors even though database-level limits (e.g., max_connections, pool size) appear adequate.  • System logs show interleaved SQL timeouts, kernel ENFILE/EMFILE or EAGAIN errors, and SYN backlog overflows.  • Performance tuning focused on any one layer yields only partial relief because pressure simply shifts among the three constrained layers.

Causal chain: Inefficient access paths inflate CPU time, I/O, and execution duration, causing each session to hold more file handles, buffers, and sockets for longer periods. This higher concurrency collides with tight OS limits on descriptors, threads, and shared memory, producing allocation failures that stall new workers and connections. Stalled or aborted connections, in turn, trigger application retries that flood the listener and network stack, exacerbating socket backlog exhaustion and increasing round-trip times. The resulting queuing further lengthens query runtimes, which feeds back into even greater resource retention on both the OS and network sides, amplifying the original schema inefficiencies and driving a self-reinforcing downward spiral in overall database performance and availability.

entry.official_definition: Aborts any statement that waits longer than the specified amount of time while attempting to acquire a lock.
entry.trigger_condition: A statement waits longer than lock_timeout for a table, index, row, or other database object lock.
entry.workload_impact: The statement attempting to acquire the lock is aborted.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
